claim.pdf_says: Table 3 — Combinations of symbols in arithmetic expressions. Its header (on page 205) is: column 1 'First symbol'; a 'Second symbol' spanning group over columns 'Identifier or literal', '+ – * / **', 'Unary + or –', '(', ')'. Page 206 carries only the five BODY rows, whose leading cell is a First-symbol value: 'Identifier or literal | — | P | — | — | P', '+ – * / ** | P | — | P | P | —', 'Unary + or – | P | — | — | P | —', '( | P | — | P | P | —', ') | — | P | — | — | P'.
claim.why_it_matters: The markdown separator line '|---|...' is placed AFTER the 'Identifier or literal' row, which promotes a First-symbol body row into a column-header row of a standalone table. Rendered, Table 3 becomes two disconnected tables and the reader cannot recover which of the five value columns is 'Identifier or literal' vs '+ – * / **' vs 'Unary + or –' vs '(' vs ')'. Table 3 is the normative statement of which operator/operand adjacencies are legal in an arithmetic expression, so an unreadable column mapping makes it unusable for deciding whether e.g. 'A + ( B' is well formed. The P/— cell values themselves are all transcribed correctly.

verdict.reasoning:
Independently verified by rendering both pages at 300 dpi and reading specs/ISO_COBOL.md around the page-205/206 anchor boundary (spec md lines ~8902-8975).

BOTH QUOTES ARE ACCURATE. PDF p.205 (printed folio 175) ends with the caption 'Table 3 — Combinations of symbols in arithmetic expressions' and the table's two-tier header only: a tall left cell 'First symbol', and a 'Second symbol' group cell spanning five sub-columns labelled 'Identifier or literal', '+ – * / **', 'Unary + or –', '(', ')'. PDF p.206 (folio 176) opens with the five body rows and no repeated header, then the in-table legend 'The letter ''P'' indicates a permissible pair of symbols. / The character ''—'' indicates an invalid pair.'

CELL VALUES: I read every printed cell off the p.206 render and all thirty match the markdown exactly — Identifier or literal (— P — — P), + – * / ** (P — P P —), Unary + or – (P — — P —), ( (P — P P —), ) (— P — — P). No data is altered or missing, so this is not a lost-text finding.

THE STRUCTURAL DEFECT IS REAL. The p.206 fragment's delimiter row genuinely sits after the first data row. Under GFM that makes 'Identifier or literal | — | P | — | — | P' the <thead> of a standalone six-column table: rendered, the normative row for First symbol = 'Identifier or literal' disappears from the body and its five verdicts are displayed as if they were column captions. Only four of Table 3's five First-symbol rows survive as data. That inverts the row/column axes of a normative adjacency matrix, which is more than cosmetic markup — it is exactly the table-integrity class the 'structural' severity exists for, not line wrapping or hyphenation.

I ALSO CHECKED THE OBVIOUS REFUTATIONS AND THEY DO NOT HOLD. (a) 'The header is merely on the previous page, so this is page-break furniture': the split itself is unavoidable given page anchors, but the defect is not the split — it is that the p.206 fragment promotes a data row instead of repeating (or emitting an empty) header row. Repeating the six column captions on p.206 fixes it with no change to any transcribed glyph. (b) 'The mapping is recoverable': partly, and this is where the claim OVERSTATES. The p.205 fragment does carry the labels in the correct order with a leading empty cell that aligns them to the six-column body — so a reader of the RAW markdown can recover the mapping from the immediately preceding lines. The claim's 'the reader cannot recover which of the five value columns is which' is therefore too strong for raw-text consumption and true only for the rendered view.

SIBLING DEFECT FOUND ON THE p.205 SIDE (not in the claim, same table, should be fixed in the same edit): the p.205 fragment is '| First symbol | Second symbol | | | |' over a FIVE-column delimiter row, followed by a SIX-cell label row '| | **Identifier or literal** | **+ – * / \*\*** | **Unary + or –** | **(** | **)** |'. GFM truncates cells beyond the declared column count, so the ')' column caption is dropped entirely when rendered. Rendered end-to-end, a reader gets four captions for six columns plus a data row masquerading as a header — which is what actually makes Table 3 unusable, and it takes both fragments to explain that.
verdict.corrected_description: CONFIRMED, with the impact restated and the scope widened to both fragments of the same table. Table 3 spans the p.205/p.206 anchor boundary: p.205 holds the caption and the two-tier header, p.206 holds the five body rows and the P/— legend. All thirty P/— cells on p.206 are transcribed correctly and no text is missing. The genuine defect is structural markup: (1) on p.206 the '|---|---|---|---|---|---|' delimiter is emitted after the first data row, so GFM renders 'Identifier or literal | — | P | — | — | P' as the table head — the First-symbol = 'Identifier or literal' row vanishes from the body and its five verdicts read as column captions, leaving only four of Table 3's five rows as data; (2) on p.205 the header row '| First symbol | Second symbol | | | |' declares five columns while the caption row beneath it carries six cells, so GFM truncates the trailing '**)**' caption out of existence. Net rendered result: six data columns labelled by at most four surviving captions, plus one normative row displayed as a header. The claim's assertion that the column mapping is unrecoverable is overstated for raw-text readers — the p.205 caption row does list the five Second-symbol labels in the correct order with a leading empty cell that aligns them to the six-cell body rows — but it is accurate for any rendered view. Fix: repeat the full six-cell column-caption row (or an equivalent flattened header such as 'First symbol | Identifier or literal | + – * / ** | Unary + or – | ( | )') above the delimiter on the p.206 fragment, and widen the p.205 delimiter row to six columns so the ')' caption is not dropped.
